title: What does fit and proper mean?
description: Fit and proper is the regulatory test of competence, honesty and integrity for people in key roles. How APRA, Solvency II, the EBA and the DFSA apply it.
shortAnswer: A fit and proper requirement is a regulatory test that people in key roles at a regulated firm, such as directors, senior managers and heads of control functions, must pass before appointment and keep meeting afterwards. Fitness covers competence: qualifications, knowledge, skills and experience for the role. Propriety covers character: honesty, integrity, good repute and financial soundness. Financial regulators in most markets apply some version, often called suitability.
keyTakeaways: Fit means competent for the specific role; proper means honest, of good repute and with integrity.
The test is applied before appointment and then reassessed, often annually, not just once.
Solvency II Article 42 requires everyone who effectively runs an insurer or holds another key function to be of good repute and have adequate professional qualifications and experience.
EU banking suitability guidelines set time limits for induction and for acquiring required knowledge after appointment.
Competence evidence for fitness is a training and assessment record, so L&D teams own part of the fit and proper file.

sections.heading: What are the two parts of a fit and proper test?

blocks.text: A fit and proper test has a competence limb and a character limb. A person can fail either: a highly qualified candidate with a history of dishonesty is not proper, and an honest candidate without the knowledge the role needs is not fit.

The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) states the criteria clearly in [Prudential Standard SPS 520](https://www.apra.gov.au/standards/sps-520) for superannuation trustees: a responsible person must possess the competence, character, diligence, experience, honesty, integrity and judgment to perform the role, and the education or technical qualifications, knowledge and skills relevant to the duties. The EU insurance rule is shorter: [Solvency II](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32009L0138) Article 42(1) says "All persons who effectively run the undertaking or have other key functions shall be of good repute and possess adequate professional qualifications and experience."

sections.heading: How do different regulators apply fit and proper requirements?

blocks.text: The concept is common across financial regulation, but who it covers, when it is assessed and what must be documented differ. The table gives examples from four regimes.

Detail for Australian superannuation boards is on [APRA SPS 510 and SPS 520](/regulations/apra-superannuation-sps-510-fit-and-proper-training), and for EU banks on [EBA internal governance and suitability](/regulations/eba-internal-governance-staff-training).

sections.heading: Are fit and proper regimes changing?

blocks.text: Yes, in several markets. In Australia, APRA consulted in 2026 on a governance package that would narrow the responsible persons subject to fit and proper requirements and rely on the [Financial Accountability Regime](/regulations/financial-accountability-regime-training) as the primary accountability mechanism; consultation closed on 28 August 2026, with new requirements expected from early 2028. In the EU, the Capital Requirements Directive as amended by CRD VI requires induction and training of management body members to include environmental, social and governance (ESG) risks and ICT risk. Check the current text before relying on any requirement.

sections.heading: What evidence of fitness should a training team keep?

blocks.text: Training teams should keep evidence that links each person's knowledge and skills to the competencies documented for their role, and that shows how gaps found at assessment were closed. A list of courses attended is weak evidence on its own.

items: The documented competencies for the position, derived from the role's responsibilities.
The assessment of the person against those competencies before appointment, with the assessor and date.
An induction and development plan for any gaps, with deadlines that match the regime (for example the EBA's one month, six month and one year markers).
Records of completed development and of how it was assessed.
The annual or periodic reassessment and its outcome.

blocks.text: A [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework) and [proficiency scale](/glossary/proficiency-scale) for board and senior roles make these assessments repeatable and comparable across people.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents the competencies for each covered role as structured, source linked requirements, with assessment points attached. Fit and proper reassessments then draw on the same evidence as development plans, and a regulatory change to the role's obligations shows which competencies and people need review.

faqs.q: Is fit and proper the same as suitability?
faqs.a: Broadly, yes. EU banking rules use suitability for the same idea, assessing knowledge, skills and experience alongside reputation, honesty and integrity. Some regimes add elements such as independence of mind or time commitment, so the label matters less than the criteria in the specific rule.

faqs.q: Does fit and proper apply to all employees?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most regimes cover directors, senior managers and key function holders. Some firms extend a lighter version to all staff, and AML rules such as Article 13 of the EU Anti-Money Laundering Regulation require integrity and skills assessments for relevant employees before they start.

faqs.q: Who carries out the fit and proper assessment?
faqs.a: The regulated firm carries out the assessment and keeps the records. Some regulators also assess or approve certain appointments themselves, and many require notification. Solvency II Article 42(2), for example, requires insurers to notify supervisors of the identity of the persons covered.

faqs.q: How often should fitness be reassessed?
faqs.a: It depends on the regime. APRA SPS 520 requires annual reassessment of responsible persons, and DFSA GEN 7.7.1 requires at least an annual review of Authorised Individuals. Reassessment should also follow a change of role or a significant event affecting propriety.
